name: The Duhem-Quine Thesis
statement: No hypothesis is tested alone: an experiment tries a whole web of assumptions at once.
statementAccent: an experiment tries a whole web of assumptions at once
meaning: The Duhem-Quine thesis, also called confirmation holism, holds that a scientific hypothesis can never be tested in isolation, because deriving any testable prediction from it requires a whole cluster of background and auxiliary assumptions, about instruments, initial conditions, and other theories. When an experiment yields a result conflicting with the prediction, logic alone does not tell us which element of the cluster is at fault: the target hypothesis, or one of the auxiliaries. A failed prediction refutes only the conjunction of all the assumptions, not any single member, so the scientist can always preserve a favored hypothesis by adjusting the auxiliaries instead. The thesis combines two related but distinct claims. The French physicist and historian of science Pierre Duhem argued, in The Aim and Structure of Physical Theory of 1906, that in physics an experiment can never condemn an isolated hypothesis but only a whole theoretical group, and that the physicist can always save a hypothesis by modifying the surrounding assumptions; Duhem restricted his thesis to physics and was skeptical of extending it. W. V. O. Quine, in his 1951 paper Two Dogmas of Empiricism, advanced a far more radical, global holism on which our statements about the world face the tribunal of experience not individually but only as a corporate body, so that any statement can be held true come what may and none, not even logic, is immune from revision.
mechanism: The Duhem-Quine thesis follows from the logic of testing. To test a hypothesis, one derives from it an observable prediction, but no interesting hypothesis entails an observation on its own; the derivation always leans on auxiliary premises, the theory of how the instruments work, assumptions about the initial and background conditions, and other accepted theories. So what actually confronts the experiment is not the hypothesis alone but the whole bundle. If the predicted observation fails to appear, standard logic, by modus tollens, tells us only that the conjunction is false, that at least one of the many premises is mistaken, without indicating which. This is the heart of the problem: the falsifying evidence is distributed over the entire cluster, and the scientist is free, as a matter of logic, to lay the blame on any member. In practice one can protect a central hypothesis by revising an auxiliary instead, a move historically illustrated when anomalies in the orbit of Uranus were met not by rejecting Newtonian mechanics but by positing an unseen planet, which turned out to be Neptune. Duhem drew the moderate conclusion, for physics, that there can be no crucial experiment decisively refuting a single hypothesis. Quine universalized the point into a picture of knowledge as a seamless web of belief that meets experience only at its edges, so that a recalcitrant observation can be accommodated by adjusting the web at many different places, guided by pragmatic considerations like simplicity and conservatism rather than by logic alone.

examples.text: A prediction follows only from a hypothesis plus auxiliaries, so an experiment tests the whole bundle, not the hypothesis alone.
Anomalies in Uranus's orbit were met by positing Neptune, not by rejecting Newton, saving the core by revising an auxiliary.
Quine held our statements face the tribunal of experience not individually but only as a corporate body.

variants.name: Duhem's moderate thesis
variants.text: Duhem's claim, restricted to physics, that an experiment condemns a whole theoretical group, never an isolated hypothesis.

variants.name: Quine's radical holism
variants.text: Quine's global thesis that all knowledge faces experience as a web and no statement is immune from revision.

whyItMatters: The Duhem-Quine thesis is one of the most important results in the philosophy of science, because it undermines the simple picture of scientific testing as a matter of confronting an isolated hypothesis with a decisive observation. By showing that hypotheses are always tested in bundles with auxiliary assumptions, it explains why there can be no truly crucial experiment that refutes one hypothesis once and for all, and why a failed prediction never dictates which belief to give up. This poses a direct challenge to naive falsificationism, since any apparent falsification can be deflected onto an auxiliary rather than the target theory, and it opens the door to legitimate, and sometimes ad hoc, rescue of theories. In Quine's radical form it reshapes epistemology itself, replacing the image of knowledge as a structure built on isolated observational foundations with the image of a web of belief that faces experience as a whole and is revisable throughout, including its logical and mathematical core. The thesis is a principal source of the underdetermination of theory by evidence and a recurring reference point in debates over confirmation, theory choice, and scientific rationality. As the insight that no hypothesis meets evidence alone, the Duhem-Quine thesis is foundational to modern philosophy of science.

working.text: note that a testable prediction follows from a hypothesis only together with background and auxiliary assumptions.
recognize that a failed prediction refutes only the conjunction, not any single member of the bundle.
see that one may save the hypothesis by adjusting an auxiliary, guided by pragmatic virtues rather than logic alone.

limits: The Duhem-Quine thesis is powerful but its scope and force are debated, and the two versions must be distinguished. Duhem confined his claim to physics and doubted its extension to other domains, whereas Quine extended holism to all of knowledge; the combined Duhem-Quine label can blur this difference. Critics of strong holism argue that in practice scientists can and do locate the source of error, that background assumptions are not all equally open to revision, and that some auxiliaries are far better supported than the hypothesis under test, so that rational blame-assignment is usually possible even though logic alone does not compel it. The thesis shows that saving a hypothesis by revising auxiliaries is always logically available, but not that every such rescue is reasonable; ad hoc, unmotivated revisions are widely judged inferior to those that yield new predictions. Some exact wordings and datings, such as Quine's paper appearing in 1951 and being reprinted in 1953, and the precise phrasing of his claims, reward checking against the sources. So the Duhem-Quine thesis robustly establishes that hypotheses are tested only in bundles, understood as a result whose radical holist version is contested and which constrains but does not abolish rational theory appraisal.
misreadings: The Duhem-Quine thesis is not the claim that theories can never be tested or that evidence is irrelevant; it is the claim that evidence bears on whole bundles of assumptions rather than isolated hypotheses. Duhem's moderate version, confined to physics, differs from Quine's radical version covering all knowledge, and running them together obscures this. And the thesis shows that saving a hypothesis by blaming an auxiliary is always logically possible, not that every such move is rational, so treating it as making testing impossible, as a single uniform doctrine, or as licensing any ad hoc rescue, misreads confirmation holism.
origin: The thesis, from Pierre Duhem's 1906 work in physics and W. V. O. Quine's 1951 Two Dogmas of Empiricism, that hypotheses are tested only in bundles with auxiliary assumptions, so no hypothesis is refuted in isolation.

sources.text: Underdetermination of Scientific Theory, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the Duhem-Quine thesis that hypotheses are tested only with auxiliary assumptions, so a failed prediction does not reveal which element is at fault, Duhem on the impossibility of a crucial experiment, Quine's radical global holism, and the differing scope of the two versions.

Pierre Duhem, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — Duhem's biography, The Aim and Structure of Physical Theory (1906), his claim that an experiment condemns only a whole theoretical group, his restriction of the thesis to physics, and Quine's extension of it to all knowledge.
